[CONCLUSION]: It was found that radiotherapy increased oxidative stress, the periodontal attachment level and alveolar bone loss, and protective melatonin administration significantly reduced the oxidative parameters and prevented periodontal damage in irradiated rats with experimental periodontitis. key_findings.finding: Direct evidence exists from a 2017 rat study (PMID 27510437) titled 'Melatonin prevents radiation-induced oxidative stress and periodontal tissue breakdown in irradiated rats with experimental periodontitis.' In 60 male Sprague-Dawley rats, groups included periodontitis plus irradiation (Ped-Rt) and periodontitis plus irradiation plus protective melatonin (Ped-Rt-Mel). Relative to Ped-Rt, melatonin significantly lowered oxidative stress index, 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, malondialdehyde, and C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen, and significantly reduced alveolar bone destruction and attachment-level damage. The abstract does not provide radiation dose or melatonin dose/timing, so those details remain unavailable from the retrieved record.

key_findings.finding: A second directly relevant study (2024; PMID 39614289) used 40 female Sprague-Dawley rats with ligature-induced periodontitis, followed the next day by a single 5-Gy radiotherapy dose; melatonin 10 mg/kg was started the same day and continued for 15 days. By day 23, compared with Ep+Rt controls, melatonin significantly limited buccal, lingual, and furcal alveolar bone loss, with destruction reported as close to control, and improved oxidative-stress, inflammatory, apoptotic, and bone-remodeling outcomes. Assays included tissue TOS/TAS, IL-1β, IL-10, IL-6, TNF-α, RANKL, OPG, and caspase-3; the paper’s conclusion attributes benefit to suppression of inflammatory stress, apoptosis, and RANKL-related osteoclastic activity. Melatonin was not statistically different from amifostine across measured parameters.
